newsitem.title: USA: Smoking verdict like watching sister die again-Raulerson.
newsitem.headline: Smoking verdict like watching sister die again-Raulerson.

text.p: Dana Raulerson said it was like watching her sister die again.

Raulerson, a 42-year-old smoker who decided to take on Big Tobacco after watching her sister, Jean Connor, wither and die of lung cancer 19 months ago, said she got a "sinking loss feeling" when a Jacksonville jury Monday absolved R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co of responsibility for her sister's death.
"It was like watching her die all over again," Raulerson said. "And there's still an industry that doesn't care she's dead because of their product."
"I don't know how they sleep at night."

Connor filed a product liability case against the tobacco giant after she was diagnosed with lung cancer, but did not live long enough to see it through. Raulerson took up the case as a wrongful death action when Connor died in October 1995 at age 49.
Connor began smoking as a teen-ager and smoked Reynolds' Salem brand cigarettes for more than two decades, switching in the mid-1980s to Benson & Hedges.

She developed a three-pack-a-day habit during more than 30 years of smoking and quit because she wanted a tummy tuck and her surgeon would not perform the operation on a smoker. She was diagnosed with cancer a few months after quitting.
"She always assumed responsibility for her part in the relationship she had with tobacco," Raulerson said. But "Jean wasn't making an adult decision when she was 14 year old."

Raulerson said the verdict, clearing Reynolds of charges that it negligently caused Connor's death by making a defective product and misleading the public about its dangers, was a sign that the American public still had not learned about the addictive nature of cigarettes.
"When you start smoking cigarettes, you're in a lifelong relationship," she said. But "we just don't seem to get it, because it's the 'legal' killer. It's the legal drug."
Raulerson said she quit smoking before the trial started but wore a nicotine patch to feed her craving. She smoked again last week, attributing her relapse to the stress of the trial.
Asked after the verdict was announced if she wanted a cigarette, Raulerson said: "If I could stick it in somebody's nose."
